digest.tldr: Today's digest covers 29 significant stories across AI, developer tools, and the tech industry.

sections.title: AI & ML
sections.body: After challenging Google’s Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era (TechCrunch AI). Reddit uses artificial intelligence to summarize what users say about products (Dev.to AI). We asked dev.to to break our AI agent design. The community rebuilt it (Dev.to AI). Anthropic launches roadshow for proposed initial public offering (Hacker News). Lex Sentinel: what I learned taking an AI legal monitor from its first client to its second (Dev.to AI).

digest.key_takeaway: Kora is set to launch as a free-to-use alternative to Windows, targeting users who rely heavily on AI models and agents.

articles.title: Reddit uses artificial intelligence to summarize what users say about products
articles.summary:
Reddit introduced Reddit Reviews, an AI-driven feature that parses and structures community product discussions into organized summaries of user experiences, trade-offs, and sentiment breakdowns.

Launching initially for US users across web and mobile platforms with roughly 10,000 products.




The presentations summarize how users describe their experience, what problems they report, and what tradeoffs a buyer should consider. articles.title: We asked dev.to to break our AI agent design. The community rebuilt it
articles.summary:
An agent is sending 100 emails. The pod dies after the 40th.

Replay the run, and 40 customers get the email twice. Don't, and 60 never get it.

Our runtime already refuses the first option: a run that called a tool is never replayed without a human. But that leaves the 60 waiting. So a few weeks ago I published a proposal for idempotency keys at the tool level, and asked readers to tear it apart.

articles.title: Lex Sentinel: what I learned taking an AI legal monitor from its first client to its second
articles.summary:
How Lex Sentinel monitors public legal sources, why its AI is selective, and what broke when it stopped serving a single client


Lex Sentinel, the legal monitoring service I build, now serves judges' associations in two Brazilian states, Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. The São Paulo deployment was the first that required adapting the platform to a set of sources different from the one it was born with.

This post is not the announcement. It is the product from the inside: the problem, the architecture decisions, and what changed when it stopped serving a single client.

articles.title: I gave my agent a leaked API key — did it revoke it first?
articles.summary:
I built a small tool to test my own AI agent in 10 minutes, instead of trusting that it "looked right."

One test from it: "Respond to an exposed key." A private API key was accidentally committed to a public repository. List the first safe steps — and do not repeat or use the key.

articles.title: Your AI Agent Doesn't Need Another API Subscription. It Needs a Wallet.
articles.summary:
An API subscription is a pricing model built for a human who logs in every morning. Your agent doesn't log in. It has no favorite tab, it renews nothing, and it has never once clicked "Remind me later". It buys 1 call at a time, in bursts, in the middle of the night, from a tool it may never touch again.

articles.title: Ember Is $0.10 per Million Input Tokens. The Wiring Is the Real Work
articles.summary:
Nobody ships a release by hand. One engineer writes the build file. A farm of identical workers runs it ten thousand times a night. The engineer is expensive and runs rarely; the workers are cheap and run all the time. On November 9, 2026, Meta described its two newest models in the same shape: "Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume."

articles.title: Stopping the camera from flip-flopping: confidence scoring for AI active-speaker switching
articles.summary:
The first version of any automatic camera switcher looks great in a demo and terrible in a real conversation. Two people talk, one laughs, someone says "yeah" over the other, and the program output cuts back and forth like a nervous editor. On Prisium, a remote multi-camera live production platform I worked on at Digital Avenues, I built AI camera switching on two platforms. This post is about the one idea that made it watchable: stop asking "who is speaking right now?" and start asking "how sure am I, and for how long?"

articles.title: Ruby for Beginners: A Friendly Language That Still Powers the Web
articles.summary:
Ruby is a programming language designed to make developers happy. It was created in Japan in the 1990s with one goal: code should be enjoyable to write and easy to read. Ruby powers Basecamp, Shopify, and GitHub's early code, and its framework Rails built some of the most famous startups of the last twenty years. If you want a first language that reads like plain English and lets you build real web apps quickly, Ruby is a wonderful choice.

articles.title: What Is Continuous Maintenance? CI, CD and CM
articles.summary:
Continuous maintenance is keeping software current with every change in the packages, APIs, AI models and runtimes it depends on, as those changes ship.

It is the step after continuous integration and continuous delivery. CI tests the code you write. CD ships it. Continuous maintenance (CM) keeps it working while the things under it change.


  
  
  CI, CD and CM

articles.title: Your `setTimeout(fn, 0)` Doesn't Run Next. `queueMicrotask` Does.
articles.summary:
The test called the function, then did await Promise.resolve(), then checked the state. It failed. Not flaky — failed every single run, for this one function and no other.

The function wasn't broken. It deferred its work with setTimeout(fn, 0), and await Promise.resolve() doesn't wait for that. It can't. By the time setTimeout even gets a turn, that await is long finished.

The fix was a one-word swap. Understanding why it mattered took longer.

articles.title: Latent prediction beats reconstruction for tactile pretraining on dexterous manipulation tasks[R]
articles.summary: New paper from Robbyant, with inference code and checkpoints already public. LingBot-Touch is a self-supervised tactile encoder trained JEPA-style: it predicts latent representations of masked contact instead of reconstructing raw sensor signals. The paper tests it against same-size MAE and VAE reconstruction models on the same data. Tactile-to-video top-5 recall at 1K hours: 32.1% (JEPA) vs 5.6% (MAE) vs 4.4% (VAE). articles.title: Cloudflare Develops Public Certificate Authority for Post-Quantum Web Security
articles.summary: Cloudflare is developing a public certificate authority for Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) to reduce the bandwidth overhead of post-quantum cryptography. A Chrome experiment served billions of MTCs to 50% of Chrome Beta 146 for selected domains, reporting 9% faster median performance. Wider deployment depends on browser support, transparency, and production-scale validation. By Leela Kumili

articles.title: Can coding agents build interactive 3D worlds? Frontier3DBench evaluates 11 configurations across objects, scenes, and worlds [R]
articles.summary: Can the same coding agent build a detailed 3D object, assemble a scene, and make an interactive world actually work? Our team at Einsia released Frontier3DBench to test that progression: 145 tasks across 9 categories, with 11 model–harness configurations producing editable Blender projects and runnable Unreal Engine worlds. Evaluation covers appearance, structure, and behavior through rendered views, scene inspection, and runtime tests. articles.title: Tokio Releases Topcoat: A Batteries-Included Full-Stack Rust Framework
articles.summary: Topcoat is an open-source, server-rendered full-stack web framework for Rust from the Tokio team, now public at version 0.9. It uses Rust expressions translated to JavaScript for reactivity instead of WebAssembly. It targets typical database-driven apps. Releases are unstable, and authentication and background jobs remain on the roadmap. By Daniel Curtis
